You already know how to do this by hand

You've already solved this question by hand, using character codes (see Learned earlier at the bottom of this page). Most languages also have ready-made helpers that test and change a letter's case, so you don't need the codes at all.

Ready-made helpers

toUpperCase() and toLowerCase() return a new string with its letters changed. They work on a one-character string too:

"q".toUpperCase();        // "Q"
"Q".toLowerCase();        // "q"
"1".toUpperCase();        // "1": not a letter, unchanged

Calling one of these on the whole string changes every letter the same way, so it can't do this question on its own: making everything uppercase and then everything lowercase just gives lowercase. Each character needs its own decision.

See MDN's toUpperCase() and toLowerCase(). These also handle letters beyond ASCII, which adding 32 doesn't.

You already know how to do this by hand

You've already solved this question by hand, using character codes (see Learned earlier at the bottom of this page). Most languages also have ready-made helpers that test and change a letter's case, so you don't need the codes at all.

Ready-made helpers

Strings have methods that test and change case. They work on a one-character string too:

"Q".isupper()             # True
"q".islower()             # True
"1".isupper()             # False: not a letter
"q".upper()               # "Q"
"Q".lower()               # "q"

Calling one of these on the whole string changes every letter the same way, so it can't do this question on its own: making everything uppercase and then everything lowercase just gives lowercase. Each character needs its own decision.

Python also has s.swapcase(), which does this whole question in one call. Try it with the per-character methods above first, then compare with swapcase(). See String Methods in the Python documentation. These methods also handle letters beyond ASCII, which adding 32 doesn't.

learning.cpp:
You already know how to do this by hand

You've already solved this question by hand, using character codes (see Learned earlier at the bottom of this page). Most languages also have ready-made helpers that test and change a letter's case, so you don't need the codes at all.

Ready-made helpers

The header <cctype> has isupper, islower, toupper and tolower. Put #include <cctype> at the top of your code. They take and return an int, and expect a value that fits in unsigned char, so the careful way to use them is:

static_cast<char>(toupper(static_cast<unsigned char>(c)))   // 'q' becomes 'Q'
isupper(static_cast<unsigned char>(c))   // nonzero if c is 'A' to 'Z'

With ASCII only, a plain char works too, but the cast to unsigned char is a good habit: for a negative char (possible above 127) their behaviour is undefined. See std::toupper on cppreference.

There's no one-call version for a whole std::string. Any "whole string" approach changes every letter the same way, so it can't do this question on its own: making everything uppercase and then everything lowercase just gives lowercase. Each character needs its own decision.

You already know how to do this by hand

You've already solved this question by hand, using character codes (see Learned earlier at the bottom of this page). Most languages also have ready-made helpers that test and change a letter's case, so you don't need the codes at all.

Ready-made helpers

The class Character (in java.lang, so no import is needed) tests and changes single characters:

Character.isUpperCase('Q');   // true
Character.isLowerCase('q');   // true
Character.isUpperCase('1');   // false: not a letter
Character.toUpperCase('q');   // 'Q'
Character.toLowerCase('Q');   // 'q'

A String also has toUpperCase() and toLowerCase().

Calling one of these on the whole string changes every letter the same way, so it can't do this question on its own: making everything uppercase and then everything lowercase just gives lowercase. Each character needs its own decision.

See Character. These also handle letters beyond ASCII, which adding 32 doesn't.

You already know how to do this by hand

You've already solved this question by hand, using character codes (see Learned earlier at the bottom of this page). Most languages also have ready-made helpers that test and change a letter's case, so you don't need the codes at all.

Ready-made helpers

The module std.ascii has isUpper, isLower, toUpper and toLower for single ASCII characters. Add import std.ascii; above your function. Writing the full name, as below, avoids mixing them up with the whole-string functions of the same names in other modules:

std.ascii.isUpper('Q');    // true
std.ascii.toLower('Q');    // 'q'

Calling one of these on the whole string changes every letter the same way, so it can't do this question on its own: making everything uppercase and then everything lowercase just gives lowercase. Each character needs its own decision.

See std.ascii in the D library reference.

Given a string s of words, spaces, digits and punctuation, return a new string in which every lowercase letter has been changed to uppercase and every uppercase letter has been changed to lowercase, both at the same time. Everything that isn't a letter stays as it is.

You've done this by hand in To Uppercase and Lowercase. This time, use the language's ready-made helpers for testing and changing case.
